Tutorial 1 · 1Position at maximum positive velocityReviewed
Link to this problem

Problem

For x = 6t² − t³ metres, find the position when velocity in the positive x direction is greatest.

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Differentiate position

    Positive-direction speed means the maximum positive velocity.

    v=12t−3t2,a=12−6tv=12t-3t^2,\qquad a=12-6tv=12t−3t2,a=12−6t

  2. Locate the maximum

    Set acceleration to zero. Velocity is a downward-opening parabola.

    a=0⇒t=2 sa=0\Rightarrow t=2\,\mathrm{s}a=0⇒t=2s

  3. Evaluate position

    Substitute the time into the original position function.

    x(2)=6(2)2−(2)3=16 mx(2)=6(2)^2-(2)^3=16\,\mathrm mx(2)=6(2)2−(2)3=16m
Result
x=16 m(D)x=16\,\mathrm m\quad\text{(D)}x=16m(D)

Check. v(2)=12 m/s and d²v/dt² = −6 < 0. Speed magnitude later grows without bound in the negative direction; that is not the requested positive-direction maximum.

Tutorial 1 · 2Acceleration of an exponential trajectoryReviewed
Link to this problem

Problem

For x = 15e^(−2t) m, find acceleration at t = 1 s.

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Differentiate once

    Velocity is negative as position decreases.

    v=−30e−2t m/sv=-30e^{-2t}\,\mathrm{m/s}v=−30e−2tm/s

  2. Differentiate again

    Acceleration is positive.

    a=60e−2t m/s2a=60e^{-2t}\,\mathrm{m/s^2}a=60e−2tm/s2

  3. Evaluate

    Use t = 1 s.

    a(1)=60e−2=8.12 m/s2a(1)=60e^{-2}=8.12\,\mathrm{m/s^2}a(1)=60e−2=8.12m/s2
Result
a=8.1 m/s2(C)a=8.1\,\mathrm{m/s^2}\quad\text{(C)}a=8.1m/s2(C)

Check. The printed choices incorrectly show m/s; acceleration must have units m/s².

Tutorial 1 · 3Displacement for half the accelerationReviewed
Link to this problem

Problem

Cart A (mass m) starts at rest with acceleration a and travels x in time t. Cart B (mass 4m) starts at rest with acceleration a/2. Find its distance in the same time.

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Write the first displacement

    With zero initial speed, displacement depends on acceleration and time.

    x=12at2x=\tfrac12at^2x=21​at2

  2. Use the second acceleration

    The given acceleration already accounts for any force or mass effects.

    xB=12(a/2)t2=x/2x_B=\tfrac12(a/2)t^2=x/2xB​=21​(a/2)t2=x/2
Result
xB=x2(B)x_B=\frac{x}{2}\quad\text{(B)}xB​=2x​(B)

Check. Doubling or quadrupling mass does not enter kinematics once acceleration is specified.

Problem

A = 12i − 16j and B = −24i + 10j. Find |C| for C = 2A − B.

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Combine components

    Subtract the entire vector B.

    C=(24,−32)−(−24,10)=(48,−42)\mathbf C=(24,-32)-(-24,10)=(48,-42)C=(24,−32)−(−24,10)=(48,−42)

  2. Compute magnitude

    Use orthogonal components.

    ∣C∣=482+(−42)2=63.78|\mathbf C|=\sqrt{48^2+(-42)^2}=63.78∣C∣=482+(−42)2​=63.78
Result
∣C∣≈64(C)|\mathbf C|\approx64\quad\text{(C)}∣C∣≈64(C)

Check. Both components contribute positively to the squared magnitude.

Problem

B + C points along +y and has magnitude |C|, where C = 3i + 4j. Find |B|.

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Find the required resultant

    C has magnitude 5, so the resultant is 5j.

    ∣C∣=5,R=(0,5)|\mathbf C|=5,\qquad\mathbf R=(0,5)∣C∣=5,R=(0,5)

  2. Subtract C

    Solve B = R − C.

    B=(−3,1),∣B∣=10=3.162\mathbf B=(-3,1),\qquad |\mathbf B|=\sqrt{10}=3.162B=(−3,1),∣B∣=10​=3.162
Result
∣B∣≈3.2(A)|\mathbf B|\approx3.2\quad\text{(A)}∣B∣≈3.2(A)

Check. (−3,1)+(3,4)=(0,5), as required.

Tutorial 1 · 6Speed under constant planar accelerationReviewed
Link to this problem

Problem

A particle starts at the origin with velocity 9.0j m/s and acceleration (2.0i − 4.0j) m/s². Find its speed when x = 15 m.

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Use horizontal position to find time

    The initial horizontal velocity is zero.

    15=12(2)t2⇒t=15=3.873 s15=\tfrac12(2)t^2\Rightarrow t=\sqrt{15}=3.873\,\mathrm s15=21​(2)t2⇒t=15​=3.873s

  2. Find both velocity components

    Acceleration changes each component independently.

    vx=2t=7.746,vy=9−4t=−6.492m/sv_x=2t=7.746,\qquad v_y=9-4t=-6.492\quad\mathrm{m/s}vx​=2t=7.746,vy​=9−4t=−6.492m/s

  3. Take the magnitude

    Speed is not the algebraic sum of components.

    v=vx2+vy2=10.11 m/sv=\sqrt{v_x^2+v_y^2}=10.11\,\mathrm{m/s}v=vx2​+vy2​​=10.11m/s
Result
v≈10 m/s(A)v\approx10\,\mathrm{m/s}\quad\text{(A)}v≈10m/s(A)

Check. The particle is moving downward at this time because vy < 0.

Tutorial 1 · 7Building height from projectile rangeReviewed
Link to this problem

Problem

A rock leaves a building at 12.2 m/s, 53° above horizontal, and lands 25 m from its base. Find the height; use g = 9.80 m/s².

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Find flight time

    Horizontal motion is uniform.

    t=2512.2cos⁡53∘=3.405 st=\frac{25}{12.2\cos53^\circ}=3.405\,\mathrm st=12.2cos53∘25​=3.405s

  2. Use vertical displacement

    Choose launch point as y = 0, so the ground is at −h.

    −h=(12.2sin⁡53∘)t−12gt2-h=(12.2\sin53^\circ)t-\tfrac12gt^2−h=(12.2sin53∘)t−21​gt2

  3. Calculate height

    Rearrange before substituting.

    h=12gt2−(12.2sin⁡53∘)t=23.63 mh=\tfrac12gt^2-(12.2\sin53^\circ)t=23.63\,\mathrm mh=21​gt2−(12.2sin53∘)t=23.63m
Result
h=23.6 m(D)h=23.6\,\mathrm m\quad\text{(D)}h=23.6m(D)

Check. The flight time exceeds the return-to-launch-level time, consistent with landing below the roof.

Tutorial 1 · 8Two positive charges from total charge and forceReviewed
Link to this problem

Problem

Two positive spheres have total charge 40 μC, are separated by 0.50 m, and repel with force 2.0 N. Find the smaller charge.

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Use Coulomb’s law

    Let the smaller charge be q.

    q(40×10−6−q)=Fr2k=5.563×10−11 C2q(40\times10^{-6}-q)=\frac{Fr^2}{k}=5.563\times10^{-11}\,\mathrm{C^2}q(40×10−6−q)=kFr2​=5.563×10−11C2

  2. Solve the quadratic

    Select the smaller positive root.

    q=40×10−6−(40×10−6)2−4Fr2/k2q=\frac{40\times10^{-6}-\sqrt{(40\times10^{-6})^2-4Fr^2/k}}{2}q=240×10−6−(40×10−6)2−4Fr2/k​​
Result
q=1.44 μC≈1.4 μC(A)q=1.44\,\mu\mathrm C\approx1.4\,\mu\mathrm C\quad\text{(A)}q=1.44μC≈1.4μC(A)

Check. The other charge is 38.56 μC; their sum is 40 μC and their Coulomb force is 2.0 N.

Problem

Place Q₂ = +80 nC at (0,0), Q₁ = +60 nC at (0,3.0 mm), and q = +24 nC at (4.0 mm,0). Find the net force magnitude on q.

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Find distances and directions

    Both forces repel q. Q₁ produces a rightward and downward force.

    r1=5.0 mm,r^1=(0.8,−0.6),r2=4.0 mmr_1=5.0\,\mathrm{mm},\quad\hat{\mathbf r}_1=(0.8,-0.6),\quad r_2=4.0\,\mathrm{mm}r1​=5.0mm,r^1​=(0.8,−0.6),r2​=4.0mm

  2. Calculate the two forces

    Use Coulomb’s law for each separation.

    F1=0.5177 N,F2=1.0785 NF_1=0.5177\,\mathrm N,\quad F_2=1.0785\,\mathrm NF1​=0.5177N,F2​=1.0785N

  3. Add components

    Take the magnitude only after adding vectors.

    F=(1.0785+0.8(0.5177),−0.6(0.5177))=(1.4927,−0.3106) N\mathbf F=(1.0785+0.8(0.5177),-0.6(0.5177))=(1.4927,-0.3106)\,\mathrm NF=(1.0785+0.8(0.5177),−0.6(0.5177))=(1.4927,−0.3106)N
Result
∣F∣=1.525 N≈1.5 N(D)|\mathbf F|=1.525\,\mathrm N\approx1.5\,\mathrm N\quad\text{(D)}∣F∣=1.525N≈1.5N(D)

Check. The resultant points about 11.8° below +x, consistent with repulsion from both positive charges.

Tutorial 1 · 10Field at the midpoint offset from two unequal chargesReviewed
Link to this problem

Problem

Q = −6.0 nC is at (0,+0.60 m), q = +3.0 nC at (0,−0.60 m), and P at (0.80 m,0). Find the electric-field magnitude at P.

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Find equal source distances

    Each charge is 1.00 m from P.

    r=0.602+0.802=1.00 mr=\sqrt{0.60^2+0.80^2}=1.00\,\mathrm mr=0.602+0.802​=1.00m

  2. Resolve each field

    The negative charge pulls the field toward upper left; the positive charge gives upper right.

    EQ=k(6×10−9)(−0.8,0.6),Eq=k(3×10−9)(0.8,0.6)\mathbf E_Q=k(6\times10^{-9})(-0.8,0.6),\quad\mathbf E_q=k(3\times10^{-9})(0.8,0.6)EQ​=k(6×10−9)(−0.8,0.6),Eq​=k(3×10−9)(0.8,0.6)

  3. Add and take magnitude

    The vertical components add while horizontal components oppose.

    E=(−21.57,48.53) N/C,E=53.11 N/C\mathbf E=(-21.57,48.53)\,\mathrm{N/C},\quad E=53.11\,\mathrm{N/C}E=(−21.57,48.53)N/C,E=53.11N/C
Result
E≈53 N/C(D)E\approx53\,\mathrm{N/C}\quad\text{(D)}E≈53N/C(D)

Check. The result points up and left, toward the larger-magnitude negative charge.

Tutorial 2 · 15Zero field outside two opposite chargesReviewed
Link to this problem

Problem

A −2.50 μC charge is at x = 0 and a +6.00 μC charge at x = 1.00 m. Find the finite point where E = 0.

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Choose the possible region

    Between opposite charges the fields point the same way. Cancellation must be left of the smaller charge.

  2. Equate magnitudes

    Let d > 0 be distance to the left of the negative charge.

    2.50d2=6.00(d+1.00)2\frac{2.50}{d^2}=\frac{6.00}{(d+1.00)^2}d22.50​=(d+1.00)26.00​

  3. Solve the distance

    Take the positive square roots.

    d=1.006.00/2.50−1=1.821 md=\frac{1.00}{\sqrt{6.00/2.50}-1}=1.821\,\mathrm md=6.00/2.50​−11.00​=1.821m
Result
x=−1.82 mx=-1.82\,\mathrm mx=−1.82m

Check. At this point the smaller negative charge is closer; the two fields have equal magnitude and opposite directions.

Problem

An aircraft is at height 2000 m; +40.0 C is at 3000 m and −40.0 C at 1000 m. Treat the concentrations as point charges and find E at the aircraft.

View original diagram / question page

    The upper positive charge pushes downward; the lower negative charge attracts downward.

  2. Add equal magnitudes

    Each source is 1000 m away.

    E=2k(40.0)(1000)2=7.190×105 N/CE=2\frac{k(40.0)}{(1000)^2}=7.190\times10^5\,\mathrm{N/C}E=2(1000)2k(40.0)​=7.190×105N/C
Result
E=−7.19×105y^ N/C(downward)\mathbf E=-7.19\times10^5\hat{\mathbf y}\,\mathrm{N/C}\quad\text{(downward)}E=−7.19×105y^​N/C(downward)

Check. The two equal contributions add rather than cancel.

Problem

A uniformly charged rod has length 0.140 m and total charge −22.0 μC. Find the field magnitude and direction on its axis 0.360 m from its center.

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Set the coordinate system

    Center the rod at the origin and evaluate at x = +0.360 m; λ = Q/L.

  2. Integrate axial contributions

    Every source-to-point displacement is along +x.

    Ex=kλ∫−L/2L/2ds(x−s)2=kQx2−(L/2)2E_x=k\lambda\int_{-L/2}^{L/2}\frac{ds}{(x-s)^2}=\frac{kQ}{x^2-(L/2)^2}Ex​=kλ∫−L/2L/2​(x−s)2ds​=x2−(L/2)2kQ​

  3. Substitute

    The negative sign indicates a field toward the rod.

    Ex=k(−22.0×10−6)0.3602−0.0702=−1.586×106 N/CE_x=\frac{k(-22.0\times10^{-6})}{0.360^2-0.070^2}=-1.586\times10^6\,\mathrm{N/C}Ex​=0.3602−0.0702k(−22.0×10−6)​=−1.586×106N/C
Result
E=1.59×106 N/Ctoward the rodE=1.59\times10^6\,\mathrm{N/C}\quad\text{toward the rod}E=1.59×106N/Ctoward the rod

Check. The result is slightly larger than k|Q|/x², and reduces to that point-charge result far away.

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

    Transverse components cancel; axial components add.

    Ex=kQx(x2+a2)3/2E_x=\frac{kQx}{(x^2+a^2)^{3/2}}Ex​=(x2+a2)3/2kQx​

  2. Evaluate near the center

    Keep all distances in metres.

    Ea=6.6408×106,Eb=2.4116×107N/CE_a=6.6408\times10^6,\quad E_b=2.4116\times10^7\quad\mathrm{N/C}Ea​=6.6408×106,Eb​=2.4116×107N/C

  3. Evaluate farther away

    All four fields point away from the positively charged ring along +x.

    Ec=6.3948×106,Ed=6.6408×105N/CE_c=6.3948\times10^6,\quad E_d=6.6408\times10^5\quad\mathrm{N/C}Ec​=6.3948×106,Ed​=6.6408×105N/C

(a) 6.64×106(b) 2.41×107(c) 6.39×106(d) 6.64×105 N/C(+x)\begin{aligned}(a)&\ 6.64\times10^6\\(b)&\ 2.41\times10^7\\(c)&\ 6.39\times10^6\\(d)&\ 6.64\times10^5\end{aligned}\ \mathrm{N/C}\quad(+x)(a)(b)(c)(d)​ 6.64×106 2.41×107 6.39×106 6.64×105​ N/C(+x)

Problem

A line extends from x₀ > 0 to infinity with linear charge density λ(x) = λ₀x₀/x. Find the electric field at the origin.

View original diagram / question page

    Charge in dx decreases with x.

    dq=λ0x0xdxdq=\frac{\lambda_0x_0}{x}dxdq=xλ0​x0​​dx

    Positive charges produce a field toward −x.

    E=−kλ0x0x^∫x0∞x−3dx\mathbf E=-k\lambda_0x_0\hat{\mathbf x}\int_{x_0}^{\infty}x^{-3}dxE=−kλ0​x0​x^∫x0​∞​x−3dx

    E=−kλ0x012x02x^\mathbf E=-k\lambda_0x_0\frac{1}{2x_0^2}\hat{\mathbf x}E=−kλ0​x0​2x02​1​x^
Result
E=−kλ02x0x^\mathbf E=-\frac{k\lambda_0}{2x_0}\hat{\mathbf x}E=−2x0​kλ0​​x^

Check. This is half the uniform-line result for the same starting density; negative λ₀ reverses direction.

Problem

Show where the magnitude of the axial field of a uniformly charged ring of radius a and charge Q is greatest, and derive its maximum value.

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Differentiate the positive-side magnitude

    Assume a > 0 and nonzero Q.

    E(x)=k∣Q∣x(x2+a2)3/2,dEdx=k∣Q∣(a2−2x2)(x2+a2)5/2E(x)=\frac{k|Q|x}{(x^2+a^2)^{3/2}},\quad \frac{dE}{dx}=\frac{k|Q|(a^2-2x^2)}{(x^2+a^2)^{5/2}}E(x)=(x2+a2)3/2k∣Q∣x​,dxdE​=(x2+a2)5/2k∣Q∣(a2−2x2)​

  2. Find the critical point

    The derivative changes from positive to negative.

    x=a2x=\frac{a}{\sqrt2}x=2​a​

  3. Substitute back

    There is an equal magnitude maximum on the negative side.

    Emax⁡=2k∣Q∣33a2=∣Q∣63πϵ0a2E_{\max}=\frac{2k|Q|}{3\sqrt3a^2}=\frac{|Q|}{6\sqrt3\pi\epsilon_0a^2}Emax​=33​a22k∣Q∣​=63​πϵ0​a2∣Q∣​
Result
∣x∣=a2,Emax⁡=∣Q∣63πϵ0a2|x|=\frac{a}{\sqrt2},\qquad E_{\max}=\frac{|Q|}{6\sqrt3\pi\epsilon_0a^2}∣x∣=2​a​,Emax​=63​πϵ0​a2∣Q∣​

Check. E vanishes at the center and tends to zero at infinity, confirming the interior extremum is the maximum.

Problem

A disk has radius 0.350 m and surface density +7.90×10⁻³ C/m². Find the field at positive axial distances (a) 0.0500 m, (b) 0.100 m, (c) 0.500 m, (d) 2.00 m.

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

    (1+R2x2)−1/2≃1−R22x2\left(1+\frac{R^2}{x^2}\right)^{-1/2}\simeq1-\frac{R^2}{2x^2}(1+x2R2​)−1/2≃1−2x2R2​

Result

Problem

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Read arrow directions

    Lines leave q₂ and terminate on q₁, so q₂ is positive and q₁ is negative.

  2. Count lines

    Six lines terminate on q₁. Eighteen lines leave q₂: six terminate on q₁ and twelve extend outward.

    ∣q1∣∣q2∣=618=13\frac{|q_1|}{|q_2|}=\frac{6}{18}=\frac13∣q2​∣∣q1​∣​=186​=31​

  3. Restore the sign

    The charges have opposite signs.

    q1q2=−13\frac{q_1}{q_2}=-\frac13q2​q1​​=−31​
Result
(a) q1q2=−13;(b) q1<0, q2>0(a)\ \frac{q_1}{q_2}=-\frac13;\qquad(b)\ q_1<0,\ q_2>0(a) q2​q1​​=−31​;(b) q1​<0, q2​>0

Check. The net positive charge explains why some lines extend to infinity.

    vp=1.5162×105 m/s,ve=6.4971×106 m/sv_p=1.5162\times10^5\ \mathrm{m/s},\qquad v_e=6.4971\times10^6\ \mathrm{m/s}vp​=1.5162×105 m/s,ve​=6.4971×106 m/s

Problem

  1. Locate possible field cancellation

    Between the charges both fields point right. To the right of −2q its field is stronger. Cancellation is possible only at x < 0, outside the smaller charge.

    kqx2=2kq(2−x)2(x<0)\frac{kq}{x^2}=\frac{2kq}{(2-x)^2}\quad(x<0)x2kq​=(2−x)22kq​(x<0)

    For x < 0, distances are −x and 2−x. Take the positive square root and solve.

    2−x=2(−x)⇒x=−2(1+2)=−4.83 m2-x=\sqrt2(-x)\quad\Rightarrow\quad x=-2(1+\sqrt2)=-4.83\ \mathrm m2−x=2​(−x)⇒x=−2(1+2​)=−4.83 m

  3. Solve the scalar potential equation

    Potentials cancel when the distance to −2q is twice the distance to +q. The absolute-value equation has one root between the charges and one to their left.

    kq∣x∣−2kq∣x−2∣=0⇒∣x−2∣=2∣x∣⇒x=−2.00 m, 23 m\frac{kq}{|x|}-\frac{2kq}{|x-2|}=0\quad\Rightarrow\quad |x-2|=2|x|\quad\Rightarrow\quad x=-2.00\ \mathrm m,\ \frac23\ \mathrm m∣x∣kq​−∣x−2∣2kq​=0⇒∣x−2∣=2∣x∣⇒x=−2.00 m, 32​ m
Result

  3. Interpret the sign

    The external agent does negative quasistatic work; 3.96 J is released during assembly.

Result

    B⊥=By2+Bz2=1.52+2.02=2.5 TB_\perp=\sqrt{B_y^2+B_z^2}=\sqrt{1.5^2+2.0^2}=2.5\ \mathrm TB⊥​=By2​+Bz2​​=1.52+2.02​=2.5 T

  2. Find force and acceleration magnitudes

    Use the elementary-charge magnitude and electron mass.

    a=evB⊥me=(1.602×10−19)(6.0×106)(2.5)9.109×10−31=2.64×1018 m/s2a=\frac{evB_\perp}{m_e}=\frac{(1.602\times10^{-19})(6.0\times10^6)(2.5)}{9.109\times10^{-31}}=2.64\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{m/s^2}a=me​evB⊥​​=9.109×10−31(1.602×10−19)(6.0×106)(2.5)​=2.64×1018 m/s2

  3. Check the force direction

    v × B has components −vBz in y and +vBy in z. Multiplication by the electron’s negative charge reverses both.

    a=evme(Bzy^−Byz^)\mathbf a=\frac{ev}{m_e}(B_z\hat{\mathbf y}-B_y\hat{\mathbf z})a=me​ev​(Bz​y^​−By​z^)
Result
a=2.6×1018 m/s2(C)a=2.6\times10^{18}\ \mathrm{m/s^2}\quad\text{(C)}a=2.6×1018 m/s2(C)

Check. Magnetic acceleration is perpendicular to velocity and changes direction rather than speed. Matches key C.

    Fz=4By=12⇒By=+3.0 TF_z=4B_y=12\quad\Rightarrow\quad B_y=+3.0\ \mathrm TFz​=4By​=12⇒By​=+3.0 T

    Bz=5.0 T,Fx=2[4(5)−6(3)]=4.0 NB_z=5.0\ \mathrm T,\qquad F_x=2[4(5)-6(3)]=4.0\ \mathrm NBz​=5.0 T,Fx​=2[4(5)−6(3)]=4.0 N
Result
By=+3.0 T(B)B_y=+3.0\ \mathrm T\quad\text{(B)}By​=+3.0 T(B)

Check. F·v = 4(2) − 20(4) + 12(6) = 0, as required for a purely magnetic force. Matches key B.

  3. Find the pitch

    The particle advances along +y during each turn.

    p=v∥T=1.88 mp=v_\parallel T=1.88\,\mathrm mp=v∥​T=1.88m
Result

Problem

A proton follows a circular path of radius 2.0 mm in B=0.25 T. Find its total distance in 1.0 s, using m=1.67×10⁻²⁷ kg and q=1.6×10⁻¹⁹ C.

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Balance radial force

    Magnetic force supplies centripetal acceleration.

    qvB=mv2r⇒v=qBrm=4.79×104 m/sqvB=\frac{mv^2}{r}\quad\Rightarrow\quad v=\frac{qBr}{m}=4.79\times10^4\,\mathrm{m/s}qvB=rmv2​⇒v=mqBr​=4.79×104m/s

  2. Use constant speed

    Magnetism changes direction without changing speed; distance is speed times time.

    s=vt=(4.79×104)(1.0)=4.79×104 ms=vt=(4.79\times10^4)(1.0)=4.79\times10^4\,\mathrm ms=vt=(4.79×104)(1.0)=4.79×104m
Result
s≈48 km(d)s\approx48\,\mathrm{km}\quad\text{(d)}s≈48km(d)

Check. Distance counts every revolution; it is not the final displacement. Matches key (d).

Result

Link to this problem

Problem

A 60 cm by 40 cm rectangular loop lies in a uniform perpendicular 0.50 T field. Starting at t=0, its length grows at 20 mm/s and width shrinks at 20 mm/s. Find emf magnitude at t=4.0 s.

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Write both time-dependent dimensions

    Use 0.020 m/s for each rate.

    ℓ(t)=0.60+0.020t,w(t)=0.40−0.020t\ell(t)=0.60+0.020t,\qquad w(t)=0.40-0.020tℓ(t)=0.60+0.020t,w(t)=0.40−0.020t

  2. Differentiate area with the product rule

    At 4 s the dimensions are 0.68 m and 0.32 m.

    dAdt=wdℓdt+ℓdwdt=0.020(w−ℓ)=0.020(0.32−0.68)=−0.0072 m2/s\frac{dA}{dt}=w\frac{d\ell}{dt}+\ell\frac{dw}{dt}=0.020(w-\ell)=0.020(0.32-0.68)=-0.0072\,\mathrm{m^2/s}dtdA​=wdtdℓ​+ℓdtdw​=0.020(w−ℓ)=0.020(0.32−0.68)=−0.0072m2/s

  3. Use Faraday’s law

    Take the magnitude of the decreasing flux rate.

    ∣E∣=B∣dA/dt∣=(0.50)(0.0072)=0.0036 V|\mathcal E|=B|dA/dt|=(0.50)(0.0072)=0.0036\,\mathrm V∣E∣=B∣dA/dt∣=(0.50)(0.0072)=0.0036V
Result
∣E∣=3.6 mV(c)|\mathcal E|=3.6\,\mathrm{mV}\quad\text{(c)}∣E∣=3.6mV(c)

Check. Equal opposite side rates do not cancel because the two dimensions are unequal. Matches key (c).

Tutorial 11 · 5Coil inside a time-varying solenoidReviewed
Link to this problem

Problem

A long solenoid has n=1500 turns/m, area 0.40 m² and current I=(4.0+3.0t²) A. A 300-turn coaxial coil of area 0.15 m² lies inside it. Find induced emf magnitude at t=2.0 s.

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Differentiate the source current

    The constant 4.0 A contributes no induction.

    dIdt=6.0t=12.0 A/s(t=2.0 s)\frac{dI}{dt}=6.0t=12.0\,\mathrm{A/s}\quad(t=2.0\,\mathrm s)dtdI​=6.0t=12.0A/s(t=2.0s)

  2. Find coil flux linkage

    The coil samples only its own area, which is smaller than the solenoid area.

    NΦ=NAcμ0nIN\Phi=N A_c\mu_0nINΦ=NAc​μ0​nI

  3. Evaluate the emf

    Differentiate the flux linkage.

    ∣E∣=NAcμ0n∣dI/dt∣=300(0.15)(4π×10−7)(1500)(12)=1.018 V|\mathcal E|=NA_c\mu_0n|dI/dt|=300(0.15)(4\pi\times10^{-7})(1500)(12)=1.018\,\mathrm V∣E∣=NAc​μ0​n∣dI/dt∣=300(0.15)(4π×10−7)(1500)(12)=1.018V
Result
∣E∣≈1.0 V(b)|\mathcal E|\approx1.0\,\mathrm V\quad\text{(b)}∣E∣≈1.0V(b)

Check. Using the solenoid’s larger area would overestimate the flux captured by the coil. Matches key (b).

Tutorial 11 · 6Steady motional induction and powerReviewed
Link to this problem

Problem

A 10 cm conducting rod slides at 2.0 m/s on frictionless conducting rails in a uniform perpendicular magnetic field. A constant applied force 0.60 N maintains the speed. The loop load is 12 Ω. Find the current magnitude.

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Use steady energy balance

    At constant speed there is no change in kinetic energy; mechanical input becomes resistor heating, assuming negligible rod/rail resistance.

    Fv=I2RFv=I^2RFv=I2R

  2. Solve for current

    The unknown field cancels, so its value is unnecessary.

    I=FvR=(0.60)(2.0)12=0.3162 AI=\sqrt{\frac{Fv}{R}}=\sqrt{\frac{(0.60)(2.0)}{12}}=0.3162\,\mathrm AI=RFv​​=12(0.60)(2.0)​​=0.3162A
Result
I≈0.32 A(a)I\approx0.32\,\mathrm A\quad\text{(a)}I≈0.32A(a)

Check. Input power is 1.2 W and I²R=1.2 W. Field direction is unspecified, so only magnitude is determined. Matches key (a).

Tutorial 11 · 7Polarity of a moving bar near a wireReviewed
Link to this problem

Problem

A horizontal bar of length L=50 cm lies a=4.0 mm above a long wire carrying 50 A to the left. The bar moves upward at v=12 m/s. End A is left and B is right. Find VA−VB.

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Find the local magnetic field

    Above a leftward current the field points into the page. All points on this parallel bar have the same distance a.

    B=μ0I2πa=(2×10−7)(50)0.0040=2.5×10−3 TB=\frac{\mu_0I}{2\pi a}=\frac{(2\times10^{-7})(50)}{0.0040}=2.5\times10^{-3}\,\mathrm TB=2πaμ0​I​=0.0040(2×10−7)(50)​=2.5×10−3T

  2. Determine charge separation

    With v upward and B into the page, v×B points left. Positive charge accumulates at A, so VA exceeds VB.

  3. Evaluate the motional voltage

    The rod is perpendicular to both velocity and field.

    VA−VB=BvL=(2.5×10−3)(12)(0.50)=0.015 VV_A-V_B=BvL=(2.5\times10^{-3})(12)(0.50)=0.015\,\mathrm VVA​−VB​=BvL=(2.5×10−3)(12)(0.50)=0.015V
Result
VA−VB=+15 mV(a)V_A-V_B=+15\,\mathrm{mV}\quad\text{(a)}VA​−VB​=+15mV(a)

Check. The positive sign follows directly from the force on positive charges toward A. Matches key (a).

Tutorial 11 · 8Voltage at the midpoint of a rotating rodReviewed
Link to this problem

Problem

A rod of total length L=0.40 m pivots at its left end P with angular speed +2.0 rad/s (counterclockwise). B=0.20 T into the page. A is its midpoint, L/2 from P. Find VA−VP.

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 3 steps

  1. Determine magnetic-force direction

    At the shown instant the rod points right and moves upward. The magnetic force on positive charges is inward toward P, making P higher in potential.

  2. Integrate over the requested part of the rod

    Local speed is ωr. Stop at A=L/2, not at the free end.

    VA−VP=∫0L/2(v×B)⋅dℓ=−∫0L/2ωBr dr=−BωL28V_A-V_P=\int_0^{L/2}(\mathbf v\times\mathbf B)\cdot d\boldsymbol\ell=-\int_0^{L/2}\omega Br\,dr=-\frac{B\omega L^2}{8}VA​−VP​=∫0L/2​(v×B)⋅dℓ=−∫0L/2​ωBrdr=−8BωL2​

  3. Insert values

    The requested voltage is one quarter of the end-to-end rod voltage.

    VA−VP=−(0.20)(2.0)(0.40)28=−0.0080 VV_A-V_P=-\frac{(0.20)(2.0)(0.40)^2}{8}=-0.0080\,\mathrm VVA​−VP​=−8(0.20)(2.0)(0.40)2​=−0.0080V
Result
VA−VP=−8.0 mV(c)V_A-V_P=-8.0\,\mathrm{mV}\quad\text{(c)}VA​−VP​=−8.0mV(c)

Check. The free-end voltage would be −32 mV; midpoint labeling is essential. Matches key (c).

Tutorial 11 · 9Ways to induce a coil currentReviewed
Link to this problem

Problem

Can a coil current be induced by (a) moving a magnet through it, (b) moving the coil toward a magnet, or (c) holding it near another coil whose current is increasing?

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Apply the flux-change criterion

    An induced emf exists when flux linkage changes; a closed conducting coil can then carry current.

    E=−d(NΦB)dt\mathcal E=-\frac{d(N\Phi_B)}{dt}E=−dtd(NΦB​)​

  2. Check all three mechanisms

    Moving either the magnet or the coil changes their relative geometry and flux. Changing current in the nearby coil changes its field and therefore the first coil’s flux.

Result
All of the above, choice (d)\text{All of the above, choice (d)}All of the above, choice (d)

Check. Motion is sufficient in (a) and (b), but changing field alone suffices in (c). Matches key (d).

Tutorial 11 · 10Lenz’s law for a falling magnetReviewed
Link to this problem

Problem

A bar magnet falls through a horizontal conducting loop, north pole downward. Viewed from above the loop, in what sequence does the induced current circulate?

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Analyze approach

    The approaching north pole increases downward magnetic flux. To oppose that increase, the loop produces an upward field: counterclockwise current viewed from above.

  2. Analyze departure

    After the magnet passes, downward flux decreases. The loop reinforces downward flux to oppose its decrease: clockwise current viewed from above.

Result
Counterclockwise first, then clockwise; choice (d)\text{Counterclockwise first, then clockwise; choice (d)}Counterclockwise first, then clockwise; choice (d)

Check. The induced magnetic force opposes the magnet’s motion in both stages. The viewing direction is explicitly from above. Matches key (d).

Problem

A 5.0 N force at 10° acts during a 2.5 m displacement at 55°. Calculate the work.

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Angle between the vectors

    Both directions use the same positive-x reference.

    θ=55∘−10∘=45∘\theta=55^\circ-10^\circ=45^\circθ=55∘−10∘=45∘

  2. Dot product

    Only the force component along displacement does work.

    W=Fdcos⁡θ=(5.0)(2.5)cos⁡45∘=8.8388 JW=Fd\cos\theta=(5.0)(2.5)\cos45^\circ=8.8388\ \mathrm JW=Fdcosθ=(5.0)(2.5)cos45∘=8.8388 J
Result
W=8.8 JW=8.8\ \mathrm JW=8.8 J

Check. The acute angle gives positive work, less than Fd = 12.5 J.

    F⃗=(5cos⁡10∘,5sin⁡10∘) N;d⃗=(2.5cos⁡55∘,2.5sin⁡55∘) m\vec F=(5\cos10^\circ,5\sin10^\circ)\ \mathrm N;\quad\vec d=(2.5\cos55^\circ,2.5\sin55^\circ)\ \mathrm mF=(5cos10∘,5sin10∘) N;d=(2.5cos55∘,2.5sin55∘) m

  2. Multiply matching components

    Cross-axis unit-vector dot products vanish.

    W=Fxdx+Fydy=8.8388 JW=F_xd_x+F_yd_y=8.8388\ \mathrm JW=Fx​dx​+Fy​dy​=8.8388 J
Result
W=8.8 JW=8.8\ \mathrm JW=8.8 J

Check. Agrees with the magnitude-and-angle method.

Problem

A 5.0 N force at 180° acts on a 2.5 m lever arm at 45°, both in the xy plane. Find the torque vector.

View original diagram / question page

Original handout page, including any printed answers. Open the PDF for full resolution.

Worked solution · 2 steps

  1. Use the order R × F

    The directed rotation from the lever toward the force is +135°.

    τz=RFsin⁡(180∘−45∘)\tau_z=RF\sin(180^\circ-45^\circ)τz​=RFsin(180∘−45∘)

  2. Magnitude and direction

    Counterclockwise rotation in the xy plane gives positive z.

    τz=(2.5)(5.0)sin⁡135∘=8.8388 N m\tau_z=(2.5)(5.0)\sin135^\circ=8.8388\ \mathrm{N\,m}τz​=(2.5)(5.0)sin135∘=8.8388 Nm
Result
τ⃗≈8.8k^ N m\vec\tau\approx8.8\hat k\ \mathrm{N\,m}τ≈8.8k^ Nm

Check. Torque is perpendicular to the lever–force plane; reversing the cross-product order would reverse its sign.
